### Phone-width captures

Headless Chrome clamps its layout viewport to a minimum width of about 500 CSS
px: `--window-size=390,1400` still lays the page out at 500 px and crops the PNG
to 390 px, so it is not a real phone rendering (the script warns when asked for
a width below 500). For a true 390 px rendering, use Chrome DevTools device
emulation (Responsive mode, 390 x 844) or the CDP method
`Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride({ width: 390, height: 844, deviceScaleFactor: 1, mobile: true })`
with `Page.captureScreenshot`. The motion on this site was checked that way at
390 px: no horizontal page overflow, and terminal blocks scroll horizontally
inside their own `<pre>` exactly as they did before the motion work.

## Motion and progressive enhancement

`motion.js` (deferred, no dependencies, no network requests) adds:

- scroll reveals for section headings, cards, figures, tables and link lists
  (IntersectionObserver; only elements below the fold are prepared, so nothing
  is hidden on load);
- terminal presentation: the existing command line is typed character by
  character, then the existing output is streamed line by line. The final text
  is identical to the HTML; nothing is invented;
- a soft shadow/border change on the sticky header after scrolling.

The hero entrance and the slow glow behind the hero are pure CSS, so they also
work without JavaScript. Accessibility and robustness:

- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` disables reveals, typing, the glow loop,
  hover lifts and transitions, and shows the final state immediately. The
  preference is re-read if the visitor changes it while the page is open.
- With JavaScript disabled, or if `motion.js` fails to load, no content is
  hidden: every page stays complete and readable.
- Animated properties are limited to `transform` and `opacity`; motion never
  affects layout, and the terminal reserves its final height before typing.
- Keyboard focus stays visible; focusing a not-yet-revealed link reveals it.

## Limits

- No trackers, cookies, analytics, third-party fonts or external assets; the
  only external links point at the repository.
- The screenshot script needs network access for the default deployed URL;
  pass a local URL for offline captures.
- Screenshot PNGs are not committed to the repository.

# Public Collaboration Templates

These are reusable starting points, not the author's live rules or project history. They contain placeholders rather than personal paths, account identifiers, or active project progress.

| Template | Role | Destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Global rules](global-AGENTS.template.md) | Stable cross-project principles, first-principles reasoning, UI hierarchy, preservation and handoff | The user-rule entry supported by your tool, or a shared rules file explicitly read by it |
| [Project rules](project-AGENTS.template.md) | Project-specific scope, structure, commands and boundaries | The project's supported rule file, commonly `AGENTS.md` |
| [Project context](CONTEXT.template.md) | Objective, facts, decisions, progress, ownership and evidence | Existing state file, or project `CONTEXT.md` when needed |

## Apply selectively

1. Inspect your existing rules and state. Choose only the missing pieces; do not overwrite existing files or introduce duplicate state.
2. Copy the chosen template to an authorized destination and replace its placeholders with verified facts. Remove unused fields instead of inventing requirements or test results.
3. Discover each tool's effective rules entry, instruction precedence and permissions. A shared Markdown file is useful only when the tool actually loads or reads it. Paths written in rules are not automatically expanded on every platform.
4. For several projects, an optional index can map project names to confirmed roots, rules and state. Keep machine-specific paths in local configuration.
5. Validate a fresh task by checking which files were read and whether the agent can identify the correct objective and next action. Report configuration separately from verified loading and handoff.

The `.template.md` suffix keeps these examples distinct from active rule files. Do not rename them in the Skill Atlas repository to activate them for all users; install adapted copies in your intended user/project location.

Agents maintain meaningful project state during authorized work. Human confirmation remains necessary for unresolved goals, permissions, and consequential actions. The context template is suitable for public fictional examples; actual context may belong in a private repository or local storage. Review it before committing, and never copy credentials or private transcripts into a public example.

For platform-specific discovery, WorkBuddy/Kimi guidance and optional checkpoint commands, see [Cross-Agent Context and Handoff](../docs/cross-agent-collaboration.md). These templates do not install hooks, switch models, dispatch tasks, or synchronize chats. No installer behavior is changed by copying this directory.

# Closeout Beginner Guide

[中文](GETTING_STARTED.zh-CN.md) | **English** | [Русский](GETTING_STARTED.ru.md)

Closeout performs evidence-based project closeout. It reconciles source code, real runtime behavior, documentation, Agent rules, authorized memory, and workspace residue.

It is not a generic file organizer and does not delete files, branches, or worktrees without informed confirmation.

## 1. Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jorgut/closeout-skill.git
cd closeout-skill
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py --all-platforms --commands
```

The last command is a preview. If no conflict is reported, apply it:

```bash
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py \
  --all-platforms \
  --commands \
  --apply \
  --confirm
```

Fully quit and reopen Codex, OpenCode, or Claude Code.

## 2. Where to Invoke It

### Codex

Codex does not expose a custom `/closeout` command. Enter:

```text
$closeout
```

Or use natural language:

```text
Use Closeout to verify that this project's code, README, and Agent rules agree.
```

### OpenCode or Claude Code

```text
/closeout
```

Natural language also works:

```text
Run Closeout on this project. Do not delete anything yet.
```

## 3. Safe First Test

Open a small Git project with code and a README, then request:

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Check only code, README, and rule files. Do not change memory or delete anything.
```

In OpenCode or Claude Code, replace `$closeout` with `/closeout`.

Read all six fact-plane statuses. If cleanup candidates are listed, nothing is deleted until you review the report and confirm specific actions.

## 4. Choose a Mode

### `docs-sync`

Use after routine development to reconcile documentation and rules with code:

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Verify startup commands, ports, and documented features against the implementation.
```

### `knowledge-closeout`

Use after completing a feature or milestone when the next session needs reliable context:

```text
$closeout knowledge-closeout. Reconcile docs, rules, and memory that this platform explicitly allows you to maintain.
```

Closeout must not write memory when no supported or authorized memory surface exists.

### `release-closeout`

Use after a PR, deployment, or release:

```text
$closeout release-closeout. Verify the separate state of code, remote repository, deployment, and live user surface.
```

Release states are distinct: `draft`, `PR`, `merged`, `deployed`, `live-verified`, `knowledge-closed`, and `cleaned`. Merged does not mean deployed, and deployed does not mean live-verified.

### `workspace-audit`

Use only when several projects must be inspected:

```text
$closeout workspace-audit. Inspect documentation and rule conflicts read-only; do not write across projects.
```

## 5. Understand the Report

| Fact plane | What it verifies |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Source, configuration, schema, and tests |
| `runtime` | What users or deployed services actually receive |
| `docs` | README and documentation accuracy |
| `rules` | AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and other active instructions |
| `memory` | Authorized cross-session knowledge |
| `workspace` | Temporary artifacts, copies, branches, or worktrees |

Statuses:

- `verified-current`: checked and correct
- `changed-and-verified`: corrected and verified again
- `pending`: evidence is unavailable; completion must not be claimed
- `out-of-scope`: excluded from this request
- `not-applicable`: the project does not have this surface

## 6. Why Cleanup Requires a Final Confirmation

Closeout first reports possible cleanup targets, such as obsolete plans, backup copies, branches, or worktrees. After reading the complete report, you must confirm the exact items to remove.

```text
User: $closeout knowledge-closeout
Agent: reports evidence and cleanup candidates
User: I reviewed the report. Delete candidates A and B, but keep C.
Agent: performs the approved cleanup, audits again, and appends the result
```

An initial request such as “finish and clean up” is not the final confirmation. This protects unique work from accidental deletion.

## 7. Useful Examples

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Verify the new login feature, environment-variable documentation, and test command.
$closeout knowledge-closeout. Prepare an accurate handoff and list unfinished work without claiming it is complete.
$closeout release-closeout. Check the GitHub commit, deployment record, and real live page; mark inaccessible evidence pending.
$closeout workspace-audit. Remain read-only and do not modify files, memory, branches, or worktrees.
```

## 8. Troubleshooting

### `/closeout` Is Missing

- Codex uses `$closeout`, not a custom slash command.
- OpenCode and Claude Code require installation with `--commands`.
- Fully restart the Agent application.
- Check command links:

```bash
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/commands/closeout.md
ls -l ~/.claude/commands/closeout.md
```

### Cleanup Candidates Were Not Deleted

This is expected. Read the pre-cleanup report and explicitly approve only the items that may be deleted.

### Why Is Something `pending`?

The Agent lacks direct evidence, such as live access, remote permissions, or executed tests. `pending` is more reliable than a false completion claim.

### Verify Installation

```bash
ls -l ~/.agents/skills/closeout/SKILL.md
ls -l ~/.codex/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.claude/skills/closeout
```

The last three paths should resolve to the same canonical installation.

# Closeout: руководство для начинающих

[中文](GETTING_STARTED.zh-CN.md) | [English](GETTING_STARTED.en.md) | **Русский**

Closeout выполняет доказательную сверку проекта после завершения этапа: сопоставляет код, реальное поведение, документацию, правила Agent, разрешённую память и остаточные файлы рабочего пространства.

Это не обычный сортировщик файлов. Он не удаляет файлы, ветки или worktree без осознанного подтверждения.

## 1. Установка

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jorgut/closeout-skill.git
cd closeout-skill
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py --all-platforms --commands
```

Последняя команда показывает план. Если конфликтов нет, примените установку:

```bash
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py \
  --all-platforms \
  --commands \
  --apply \
  --confirm
```

Полностью закройте и снова откройте Codex, OpenCode или Claude Code.

## 2. Где вводить команду

### Codex

В Codex нет пользовательской команды `/closeout`. Используйте:

```text
$closeout
```

Или обычный запрос:

```text
Используй Closeout и проверь, соответствуют ли друг другу код, README и правила Agent.
```

### OpenCode или Claude Code

```text
/closeout
```

Также можно написать:

```text
Выполни Closeout для этого проекта, но пока ничего не удаляй.
```

## 3. Первый безопасный тест

Откройте небольшой Git-проект с кодом и README, затем введите:

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Проверяй только код, README и файлы правил. Не меняй память и ничего не удаляй.
```

В OpenCode или Claude Code замените `$closeout` на `/closeout`.

Прочитайте статусы всех шести плоскостей фактов. Если указаны кандидаты на удаление, они останутся на месте до отдельного подтверждения после отчёта.

## 4. Выбор режима

### `docs-sync`

Для обычного завершения разработки и сверки документации:

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Сверь команды запуска, порты и описанные функции с текущей реализацией.
```

### `knowledge-closeout`

После завершения функции или этапа, чтобы следующая сессия получила точный контекст:

```text
$closeout knowledge-closeout. Синхронизируй документацию, правила и только ту память, которую платформа явно разрешает изменять.
```

Без поддерживаемого и разрешённого интерфейса Closeout не должен самостоятельно записывать память.

### `release-closeout`

После PR, развёртывания или релиза:

```text
$closeout release-closeout. Отдельно проверь состояние кода, удалённого репозитория, развёртывания и реального пользовательского интерфейса.
```

Состояния различаются: `draft`, `PR`, `merged`, `deployed`, `live-verified`, `knowledge-closed`, `cleaned`. Слияние не означает развёртывание, а развёртывание не означает проверку живой системы.

### `workspace-audit`

Только для проверки нескольких проектов:

```text
$closeout workspace-audit. Только читай и ищи конфликты документации и правил; не записывай изменения в соседние проекты.
```

## 5. Как читать отчёт

| Плоскость | Что проверяется |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Исходный код, конфигурация, schema и тесты |
| `runtime` | Что реально получают пользователи или сервисы |
| `docs` | Точность README и документации |
| `rules` | AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md и другие активные инструкции |
| `memory` | Разрешённые знания между сессиями |
| `workspace` | Временные файлы, копии, ветки и worktree |

Статусы:

- `verified-current`: проверено и актуально
- `changed-and-verified`: исправлено и повторно проверено
- `pending`: доказательств недостаточно, завершение заявлять нельзя
- `out-of-scope`: не входит в текущую задачу
- `not-applicable`: для проекта эта плоскость отсутствует

## 6. Почему для очистки нужно отдельное подтверждение

Сначала Closeout показывает полный отчёт и кандидатов на очистку: старые планы, резервные копии, ветки или worktree. После чтения отчёта пользователь подтверждает конкретные элементы.

```text
Пользователь: $closeout knowledge-closeout
Agent: показывает доказательства и кандидатов на удаление
Пользователь: Я прочитал отчёт. Удали A и B, но сохрани C.
Agent: выполняет разрешённую очистку, повторно проверяет проект и дополняет отчёт
```

Первоначальная фраза «заверши и почисти» не является финальным подтверждением. Это защищает единственные экземпляры работы от случайного удаления.

## 7. Примеры

```text
$closeout docs-sync. Проверь новую авторизацию, описание переменных среды и команду тестирования.
$closeout knowledge-closeout. Подготовь точную передачу проекта и перечисли незавершённое без ложных заявлений.
$closeout release-closeout. Проверь commit GitHub, запись развёртывания и живую страницу; недоступное отметь pending.
$closeout workspace-audit. Работай только на чтение и не меняй файлы, память, ветки или worktree.
```

## 8. Устранение неполадок

### Нет `/closeout`

- В Codex используйте `$closeout`.
- В OpenCode и Claude Code установщик должен запускаться с `--commands`.
- Полностью перезапустите приложение.
- Проверьте ссылки:

```bash
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/commands/closeout.md
ls -l ~/.claude/commands/closeout.md
```

### Кандидаты не были удалены

Это нормальная защита. Прочитайте предварительный отчёт и явно подтвердите только разрешённые элементы.

### Почему указан `pending`?

Нет прямого доказательства: доступа к production, прав на удалённый репозиторий или выполненных тестов. Честный `pending` надёжнее ложного статуса завершения.

### Проверка установки

```bash
ls -l ~/.agents/skills/closeout/SKILL.md
ls -l ~/.codex/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.claude/skills/closeout
```

Последние три пути должны вести к одному основному экземпляру.

# Closeout 新手使用教程

**中文** | [English](GETTING_STARTED.en.md) | [Русский](GETTING_STARTED.ru.md)

Closeout 用于项目完成一个阶段后的“事实收尾”：核对代码、实际运行结果、文档、Agent 规则、获准维护的记忆和工作区残留是否一致。

它不是普通的文件整理工具，也不会在未经确认时删除文件、分支或 worktree。

## 1. 安装

打开终端，逐行运行：

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jorgut/closeout-skill.git
cd closeout-skill
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py --all-platforms --commands
```

第三条命令只显示安装计划。确认没有路径冲突后再正式安装：

```bash
python3 scripts/install_closeout.py \
  --all-platforms \
  --commands \
  --apply \
  --confirm
```

安装后完全退出并重新打开 Codex、OpenCode 或 Claude Code。

## 2. 在哪里输入命令

### Codex

Codex 不会显示自定义 `/closeout`。在对话框输入：

```text
$closeout
```

或者直接说：

```text
使用 Closeout 检查这个项目的代码、README 和 Agent 规则是否一致。
```

### OpenCode 或 Claude Code

在对话框输入：

```text
/closeout
```

也可以使用自然语言：

```text
净化一下这个项目，先不要删除任何文件。
```

## 3. 第一次安全试用

建议先在一个有 Git、README 和少量代码的小项目里测试。

1. 用 Agent 打开项目目录。
2. 确保项目当前改动已经保存。
3. 输入：

```text
$closeout docs-sync，只核对代码、README 和规则文件，不修改记忆，不删除任何内容。
```

OpenCode/Claude Code 使用：

```text
/closeout docs-sync，只核对代码、README 和规则文件，不修改记忆，不删除任何内容。
```

4. 阅读报告中的六个事实面状态。
5. 如果报告列出删除候选，不确认就不会删除。

## 4. 四种模式怎么选

### `docs-sync`：只同步文档和规则

适合日常开发结束：

```text
$closeout docs-sync，检查 README 里的启动命令、端口和功能是否与代码一致。
```

### `knowledge-closeout`：完整知识收尾

适合一个功能或阶段完成，需要给下次会话留下准确上下文：

```text
$closeout knowledge-closeout，同步文档、规则和当前平台允许维护的记忆。
```

没有明确授权或平台入口时，Closeout 不应自行写入记忆。

### `release-closeout`：发布收尾

适合 PR 合并、部署或正式发布：

```text
$closeout release-closeout，确认代码、远端、部署和线上页面分别处于什么状态。
```

Closeout 会区分：

- `draft`
- `PR`
- `merged`
- `deployed`
- `live-verified`
- `knowledge-closed`
- `cleaned`

“已经合并”不等于“已经部署”，“已经部署”也不等于“线上验证通过”。

### `workspace-audit`：检查多个项目

只有确实要审查整个 workspace 时才使用：

```text
$closeout workspace-audit，只读检查这些项目的规则和文档冲突，不跨项目写入。
```

## 5. 如何读懂结果

Closeout 会给六个事实面分别标状态：

| 事实面 | 检查内容 |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | 源码、配置、schema 和测试实际实现了什么 |
| `runtime` | 用户或线上服务当前真正得到什么 |
| `docs` | README 和文档是否准确 |
| `rules` | AGENTS.md、CLAUDE.md 等规则是否有效 |
| `memory` | 获准维护的跨会话记忆是否准确 |
| `workspace` | 临时文件、旧副本、分支或 worktree 是否仍需处理 |

常见状态：

- `verified-current`：已经核对，当前正确
- `changed-and-verified`：已修正并重新验证
- `pending`：目前无法验证，不能假装完成
- `out-of-scope`：不属于本次范围
- `not-applicable`：这个项目不适用，例如没有部署环境

## 6. 删除和清理为什么要确认两次

Closeout 会先给出完整报告和删除候选，例如旧计划、备份副本、临时 worktree。只有你看完报告后再次明确确认，它才能执行清理。

正确流程：

```text
用户：$closeout knowledge-closeout
Agent：给出事实报告和待删除候选
用户：我已阅读报告，确认只删除候选 A 和 B，保留 C
Agent：执行删除，再重新审计并补充结果
```

最初一句“做完顺便清理”不能替代最终确认，这是为了避免误删唯一副本。

## 7. 实用示例

### 功能开发结束

```text
$closeout docs-sync，核对刚完成的登录功能、环境变量说明和测试命令。
```

### 准备交接给同事

```text
$closeout knowledge-closeout，为新接手者准备准确的项目状态；列出未完成事项，但不要编造完成状态。
```

### 发布后检查

```text
$closeout release-closeout，检查 GitHub 提交、部署记录和真实线上页面；无法访问的项目标 pending。
```

### 只检查，不修改

```text
$closeout workspace-audit，全程只读，不修改文件、记忆、分支或 worktree。
```

## 8. 常见问题

### 输入 `/` 看不到 Closeout

- Codex 使用 `$closeout`，不会显示自定义 `/closeout`。
- OpenCode/Claude Code 安装时必须带 `--commands`。
- 安装后需要完全重启应用。
- 检查命令软链接：

```bash
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/commands/closeout.md
ls -l ~/.claude/commands/closeout.md
```

### Closeout 没有自动删除候选文件

这是正常安全机制。先阅读预清理报告，再明确回复允许删除哪些项目。

### 为什么有 `pending`

`pending` 表示缺少真实证据，例如无法访问线上环境、没有权限读取远端或测试未运行。它比虚假的“全部完成”更可靠。

### 如何确认本机安装成功

```bash
ls -l ~/.agents/skills/closeout/SKILL.md
ls -l ~/.codex/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.config/opencode/skills/closeout
ls -l ~/.claude/skills/closeout
```

如果后三项显示指向同一个 canonical 目录的软链接，说明多平台正在共享同一份 Skill。

# Local Agent Environment Scan

`agents scan` is a read-only discovery command added in `0.8.0-beta`. It
answers a narrow question: which coding-agent tools leave evidence on this
machine, which rule and skill roots does each tool's documentation or
convention point at, and do the local Skill Atlas copies agree on a version?

The scan only reads filesystem metadata and local Skill Atlas `skill.json`
manifests. It never executes an agent tool, opens a network connection, reads
credentials or session data, or writes, links, or deletes anything. Its output
is **discovery evidence**, not proof that any tool is installed correctly,
configured for a project, or currently loading the files it points at.

## What the scan does and does not prove

The scan reports:

- a reviewed catalog of coding-agent tools and the paths each one conventionally
  uses for home roots, rule/instruction entries, project rules, and skill roots;
- whether each of those paths exists, is a symlink, is broken, is readable, and
  (for skill roots) how many visible child directories it contains;
- whether each tool's executable name is found in the supplied `PATH`
  (existence only, never executed);
- shared skill roots: the same physical directory reached through more than one
  tool's skill-root path;
- local Skill Atlas copies under scanned skill roots, their manifest versions,
  and a `version_mismatch` flag when copies disagree;
- explicit limitations in every result.

The scan does **not** prove:

- that a tool is installed, healthy, or running;
- that a tool loaded, read, or honored any of the reported files;
- the tool's version (no tool version command is run);
- that a Skill Atlas copy is the one a given tool actually resolves at runtime;
- that candidate paths are current, correct, or supported by the tool's own
  documentation.

Missing, unreadable, or broken paths are reported as evidence and notes; they
do not abort the scan.

## Evidence levels

Every tool gets exactly one level. These are **file-evidence levels**, never
runtime states:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `not-detected` | No tool-specific evidence was found in the scan scope. Shared skill roots alone do not change this. |
| `detected` | At least one tool-specific path or executable exists. Candidate-only evidence can produce `detected`, but never `configured`. |
| `configured` | A **documented** instruction entry exists, or the tool is otherwise detected and a **documented** skill root contains at least one skill. |

`configured` means documented configuration evidence exists on disk. It is not
`loaded` and not `handoff-verified`; those claims still require runtime evidence
from the tool itself. A present rule file is not loading, and a present skill
root is not proof that a tool reads it.

Two important consequences:

- A shared root such as `~/.agents/skills` can be listed for several tools but
  is not tool-specific evidence. It cannot by itself make a tool `detected` or
  `configured`.
- A candidate path that happens to exist only supports `detected`. Only paths
  explicitly documented in this repository can reach `configured`.

## Skill Atlas copy audit

The scan looks for a `skill-atlas/` directory under the catalog's skill roots
plus one extra conventional root, `~/.cc-switch/skills`. For each copy it:

- groups aliases that resolve to the same physical directory, so symlinked or
  duplicate roots are reported once with `aliases` and a `target`;
- reads only that copy's `skill.json` to report its `version`;
- marks the copy `readable: false` when the manifest is missing or unreadable,
  in which case `version` is `null`;
- sets `version_mismatch: true` only when at least two different readable
  versions are found.

A mismatch is a maintenance hint, not proof of which copy any tool loads. Use
the tool's own resolution behavior and the [cross-agent verification
levels](cross-agent-collaboration.md) before rewriting links or installations.
The scan never repairs, links, or deletes copies.

## Security and privacy

- **Read-only.** The scan creates, modifies, and deletes nothing. It does not
  run installers, link files, or execute agent tools.
- **No network.** No socket is opened; the catalog is local and the scan is
  offline.
- **No credential or session reads.** It inspects filesystem metadata and reads
  only `skill.json` manifests of local Skill Atlas copies. It does not read
  credential files, auth stores, session logs, chat history, or model
  configuration contents.
- **Sensitive paths.** Output contains absolute home and project paths. Redact
  them before sharing scan output publicly or attaching it to an issue.
- **Not a security boundary.** `--home` and environment overrides control scan
  scope, not access. The scan is diagnostic evidence for an authorized local
  environment.

## Limitations and how to verify a tool

The fixed limitations are the authoritative caveats:

1. **Runtime loading was not verified.** Existing files and directories do not
   prove any tool loaded them.
2. **No agent tool was executed and no tool versions were read.** A `PATH` hit
   only proves an executable file exists.
3. **Candidate paths and home overrides are unverified hints.** They may be
   version-specific or outdated.
4. **No network, credentials, or writes occurred.** No files or links were
   created or modified.
5. **`configured` is documented configuration evidence only.** `loaded` and
   `handoff-verified` remain out of scope.
6. **Project rule candidates are project-scoped hints.** Their presence does
   not prove a tool is installed or active.

To verify a tool for real:

1. Check that tool's own current documentation and version command — the
   catalog may lag a tool's actual behavior.
2. Start a fresh session with the tool and confirm which instruction and skill
   files it reports loading.
3. Distinguish **configured** (files exist), **loaded** (the tool demonstrably
   read them), and **handoff-verified** (a receiving agent correctly used the
   project objective, ownership, and next action).
4. Only then claim runtime behavior. Never upgrade scan output to a loading or
   handoff claim.

## Relation to the cross-agent workflow

Use the scan as the read-only evidence-gathering step described in
[Discover before configuring](cross-agent-collaboration.md#discover-before-configuring).
It collects candidate tool entries and roots before any configuration is
proposed; it does not configure anything and does not verify a handoff. The
catalog marks a path `documented` only when this repository's documentation
describes it, so candidate paths must be checked against the participating
tool's installed version first.

The scan is also independent of the optional local message transport
([Agent Handoff Messages](agent-messaging.md)): it never sends a message,
starts an agent, or checks an inbox.

# Agent Handoff Messages

`message` is an optional, local file-based transport for short handoff notes
between agents and people working in the same project checkout. It was added in
`0.7.0-beta`. Messages are written under `.agent-state/messages/<task>/` inside
the receiving project's Git root and are read explicitly with the commands
below.

**What it is not:**

- not a message bus, queue service, or daemon;
- not network transport: it opens no sockets, sends no telemetry, and calls no
  external service;
- not an agent dispatcher: it never starts, resumes, wakes, or notifies the
  recipient, and it never performs the requested work;
- not live chat synchronization and not a substitute for human decisions.
  A message marked `--requires-approval` cannot be recorded as `completed`
  until a person runs `message approve`.

The transport only records intent and receipts. A receiving agent still has to
run `inbox`, decide whether to accept the work, and acknowledge it. A person
still decides whether a flagged message may complete, and merges, deployments,
and other protected actions keep their normal review and permission gates.

This is a Stage 1.5 slice of the multi-agent plan: local transport and explicit
acknowledgements. The Stage 2 orchestrator is still not implemented; see
[the two-stage development plan](multi-agent-development.md).

## Quickstart

Run these steps inside the project Git repository. `--project .` is the default
for most commands, but it is shown explicitly here.

```bash
# 1. Record the task checkpoint first (existing command, unchanged)
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py checkpoint --project . --task issue-28 \
  --agent Codex --summary "Camera control implemented" \
  --completed "Camera basics" --remaining "Object selection" \
  --next-action "Review the camera diff"

# 2. Queue one compact message. Nothing is sent or delivered yet.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message send --project . --task issue-28 \
  --from Codex --to "Claude Code" \
  --summary "Review the camera diff" \
  --conclusion "Camera works; selection remains" \
  --evidence src/camera.ts --requires-approval
# Prints the new message ID, for example msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef

# 3. The recipient reads its inbox. This is a read-only local read.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message inbox --project . --task issue-28 \
  --agent "Claude Code"

# 4. The recipient shows the full envelope and receipts when it decides to act.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message show --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id <message-id>

# 5. The recipient acknowledges what actually happened.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message ack --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id <message-id> --agent "Claude Code" --status taken --note "reviewing"

# 6. For a flagged message, a person records approval before completion.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message approve --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id <message-id> --by "AJ" --note "review approved"

# 7. Only now can the recipient record completion.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message ack --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id <message-id> --agent "Claude Code" --status completed --note "merged to main"
```

`--project` must resolve to a Git repository. A non-Git directory is refused.
Message IDs and task-scoped history are local to this checkout; they are never
transferred automatically to another machine.

## Command reference

All five actions accept `--project`, `--task`, and `--format markdown|json`.
Markdown is the default. Invalid, conflicting, or refused operations exit with
status 2 and a message on stderr; the local state is not changed.

| Command | Purpose | Key flags |
|---|---|---|
| `message send` | Queue one compact message for another agent or person | `--from NAME`, `--to NAME`, `--summary TEXT` (required); `--conclusion TEXT`, `--evidence PATH` (repeatable), `--request-id ID`, `--ttl-hours HOURS` (default 24), `--reply-to MESSAGE_ID`, `--pass N`, `--requires-approval` |
| `message inbox` | List messages addressed to one agent; read-only | `--agent NAME` (required); `--status active\|all\|queued\|taken\|completed\|refused` (default `active`), `--include-expired` |
| `message show` | Show one message with its local receipts; read-only | `--id MESSAGE_ID` (required) |
| `message ack` | Record `taken`, `completed`, or `refused` | `--id MESSAGE_ID`, `--agent NAME`, `--status taken\|completed\|refused`, `--note TEXT` |
| `message approve` | Record a person's approval for a message that requires it | `--id MESSAGE_ID`, `--by PERSON`, `--note TEXT` |

Recipient names are matched case-insensitively, while the stored display name is
preserved. An agent name must start with a letter or digit and use at most 64
letters, digits, spaces, dots, dashes, underscores, or colons. A task ID uses at
most 80 letters, digits, dots, dashes, or underscores.

`send` notes:

- `--summary` is the one-line handoff. `--conclusion` is a short conclusion, not
  a transcript. `--evidence` takes short local pointers (paths, commit SHAs,
  issue numbers) and may be repeated.
- `--request-id` makes retries safe. Repeating the same request ID with the same
  content and options returns `duplicate` and the original message instead of
  creating a second message. Reusing the request ID with different content or
  options is refused. When omitted, an `auto-...` ID is generated.
- A retry is resolved before the reply chain is validated, so it still returns
  the original message after the parent has expired or been refused.
- `--reply-to` answers an existing message in the same task. The chain pass is
  derived automatically (`parent pass + 1`); `--pass` is only for validating or
  supplying that number explicitly.
- `--requires-approval` marks the message for the human approval gate.

`inbox` notes:

- The default `active` view hides terminal (`completed`, `refused`) and expired
  messages. `--status all` includes terminal messages; expired open messages are
  included only with `--include-expired`.
- At most 200 messages are returned per call; `truncated` is reported when more
  matched. Nothing is modified.

`approve` notes:

- Only a message sent with `--requires-approval` can be approved; approving any
  other message is refused.
- Expired or already terminal messages cannot be approved. Only one approval
  record is accepted: repeating it for the same person returns `duplicate`, and
  a different approver is refused so that the recorded person can confirm.

## States, receipts, and idempotency

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queued` | Written by the sender. No recipient action yet. |
| `taken` | The addressed recipient acknowledged taking the work. |
| `completed` | The addressed recipient recorded completion. If the message requires approval, a recorded approval must exist first. |
| `refused` | The addressed recipient declined the message. |
| `expired` | Derived, not stored: an open message whose `expires_at` has passed. `show` reports `status: expired`; `inbox` hides these by default; `ack` and `approve` are refused. |

The lifecycle is `queued` → `taken` → `completed` or `refused`; a recipient may
also record `completed` or `refused` directly from `queued`. Terminal statuses
cannot be changed, and repeating the same acknowledgement returns `duplicate`
without writing again. Only the addressed recipient may acknowledge a message.

Each message has an immutable JSON envelope plus separate mutable state, so an
acknowledgement never rewrites what the sender wrote. Every transition appends
one event to `receipts/<message-id>.jsonl` (`queued`, `taken`, `completed`,
`refused`, `approved`). Receipts are append-only local records, written under a
writer lock; they are evidence, not a tamper-proof audit log.

## Data layout

```text
<project-git-root>/.agent-state/
├── .lock                              # local writer lock (shared with checkpoints)
└── messages/
    └── <task>/
        ├── envelopes/<message-id>.json   # immutable message content
        ├── status/<message-id>.json      # current state, rewritten atomically
        ├── requests/<request-id>.json    # idempotency records
        ├── receipts/<message-id>.jsonl   # append-only transition events
        └── approvals/<message-id>.json   # person approval records, when required
```

The transport creates files only under `.agent-state/messages/`, never inside
your source tree. Keep message state out of Git: this repository ignores
`.agent-state/messages/` and `.agent-state/.lock`; in another project, add
those paths to `.gitignore` before creating state. Checkpoint files under
`.agent-state/tasks/` and `.agent-state/history/` keep their documented
behavior and may still be committed deliberately when a task must move between
machines. Committed or pushed message state is not the intended usage and may
expose project details.

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Default TTL | 24 hours |
| Maximum TTL | 720 hours (30 days) |
| Message chain | 10 passes; a further reply is refused |
| Inbox results per call | 200 (with truncation flag) |
| Messages per task | 5000 |
| Summary / conclusion / note | 2000 / 4000 / 2000 characters |
| Evidence entries | 20, each at most 300 characters |
| Task ID / request ID | 80 / 128 characters with restricted character sets |

A long exchange is a signal to stop and ask the user rather than continue
replying. The pass limit exists to bound local message chains, not to substitute
for task ownership.

## Safety and privacy

- **Local only.** No network calls, no telemetry, and no credential access. The
  transport never starts another agent and never executes the requested action.
- **No secrets.** Envelopes, status files, receipts, and approvals are plain
  JSON/JSONL on disk. Do not put API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, full
  file contents, or session transcripts in a payload. Use short pointers and
  summaries instead.
- **Uncommitted message state.** `.agent-state/messages/` must stay uncommitted.
  It is a local working record; checkpoints follow their own documented rule.
- **Approval is a local label, not an identity check.** `message approve --by`
  records the name a person supplies; the tool does not authenticate that
  person. Do not approve on someone else's behalf, and do not treat an approval
  as a merge, deployment, or security sign-off.
- **No delivery guarantee.** A queued file does not mean the recipient read it.
  Only the recipient's own `ack` shows that. Do not report a message as
  delivered, taken, or completed without the corresponding local receipt.
- **No symlinked state paths.** The transport refuses to use an `.agent-state`
  tree, message subdirectory, or lock file that resolves through a symlink, so a
  repository cannot redirect message state outside its Git root.
- **Shared filesystem caveat.** Anyone with write access to the checkout can
  edit these local files. Treat receipts as local evidence, not as an
  audit-grade ledger.

## Worked example: Codex → Claude Code review with human approval

Scenario: `issue-28` needs a camera-control review. Codex implemented the change
and hands a compact review request to Claude Code. A person must approve before
the message can be completed, and the merge remains a separate human action.

```bash
# Codex: record the milestone, then queue the review request.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py checkpoint --project . --task issue-28 \
  --agent Codex --summary "Camera control implemented" \
  --completed "Camera basics" --remaining "Object selection" \
  --next-action "Review the camera diff"
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message send --project . --task issue-28 \
  --from Codex --to "Claude Code" \
  --summary "Review camera diff before merge" \
  --conclusion "Camera control works; selection is not started" \
  --evidence src/camera.ts --evidence "commit $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  --requires-approval
# Response includes the message ID, for example:
# - id: msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef

# Claude Code (or the person operating it): read and inspect the message.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message inbox --project . --task issue-28 \
  --agent "Claude Code"
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message show --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef

# Claude Code: accept the review and record the outcome.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message ack --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef --agent "Claude Code" \
  --status taken --note "reviewing camera diff"

# Claude Code: reply with the review result; the pass becomes 2 automatically.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message send --project . --task issue-28 \
  --from "Claude Code" --to Codex \
  --summary "Review complete: one fix needed" \
  --conclusion "Transform math is correct; add a null check in camera.ts" \
  --evidence src/camera.ts \
  --reply-to msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef

# Codex: read the reply when it next checks its inbox.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message inbox --project . --task issue-28 \
  --agent Codex --status all

# A person reviews the change and records approval for the flagged message.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message approve --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef --by "AJ" --note "review approved"

# Claude Code: only now can completion be recorded. The merge is separate.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py message ack --project . --task issue-28 \
  --id msg_20261111T120000_ab12cd34ef --agent "Claude Code" \
  --status completed --note "fix applied; merged after review"
```

What this example does **not** do: it does not wake Claude Code, prompt a model,
merge the branch, or notify anyone. Each step runs because a person or an
already-running agent chose to run it. If Claude Code never checks its inbox,
the message simply stays `queued` until its TTL expires.

## Local project root audit

The unified CLI includes a read-only `projects audit` command for duplicated
project copies and divergent project documents:

```bash
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py projects audit \
  --project . --project /path/to/other-copy
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py projects audit \
  --root ~/Projects --depth 2 --format json
```

`--root` searches descendants only; the root itself is not reported (use
`--project` for it). `--depth` limits discovery: direct children are depth 1,
and the default is 2. The audit groups copies as confirmed (normalized git
remote, compared case-insensitively) or probable (case-folded directory name),
hashes the listed agent-facing project documents up to 256 KiB without printing
their contents, and flags divergent documents and nested project roots. It never
runs git (`.git/config` and `.git/HEAD` are parsed by hand), writes nothing, and
makes no network calls. Recommendations are plans requiring user confirmation.
See [Project Root and Duplicate Documentation Audit](project-root-audit.md) for
identity rules, the hash cap, output contract, and limitations.

## Local disk usage audit

The unified CLI includes a read-only `disk scan` command for agent homes,
caches, sessions, plugins, project media, build artifacts, and Git objects:

```bash
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan \
  --root ~/Documents/ChatGPT --root ~/Documents/Codex --min-file-mb 100
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan --project . --format json
```

Flags: `--home PATH` (known-root base, default user home), repeated
`--root PATH`, `--project PATH`, `--top N` (default 15, bounded to 0–100),
`--min-file-mb N` (default 200; files whose allocated size is at or above),
`--max-entries N` (default 400000, per-root safety limit), `--apply` (move step;
requires `--to-trash` and `--confirm`), `--to-trash`, `--confirm`, repeated
`--risk low|medium` (cleanup risks; default `low`), `--trash-dir PATH` (default
`~/.Trash`; must exist), and `--format markdown|json`. Sizes are reported as
allocated bytes (`st_blocks × 512`, the real disk usage) with apparent bytes
(`st_size`) in parentheses when they differ; the largest-files threshold,
ordering, and risk totals use allocated bytes. The scan reads metadata only,
never follows symlinks while walking, and by default never deletes, moves,
compresses, or archives anything. With `--apply --to-trash --confirm` it moves
selected low/medium risk direct-child candidates into the trash directory
(unique names, never `rm -rf`, high-risk entries and symlinks never moved) and
space is freed only after the Trash is emptied. Categories, risk levels, and
suggested actions are name-based heuristics and plans, not cleanup. See
[Disk Usage Audit](disk-scan.md) for known roots, categories, the JSON contract,
the `apply` result, and limitations.

## Checkpoints, handoff, and Git sync status

`checkpoint` and `handoff` save task evidence locally under `.agent-state/`; `resume` reads it back
without changing anything. Since `0.11.0-beta` their JSON results include a read-only
`git.sync` block and a top-level `warnings` array so unpushed work is visible in the handoff
evidence:

```bash
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync status --project .
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync status --project . --format json
```

`sync status` reports:

- `branch`, `upstream`, `has_upstream`, `ahead`, `behind`, `dirty`, `detached`, `last_commit`, `commit`;
- `warnings` for no upstream, unpushed commits (`ahead`), a remote-tracking branch ahead
  (`behind`), uncommitted changes (`dirty`), and detached HEAD;
- `tracking_refs_may_be_stale` and a note that no fetch or network call was made.

Markdown prints `# Git sync status`, the branch, upstream (or `none`), ahead/behind/dirty counts,
each warning, and the read-only note. JSON returns
`{status: "ok", project, git: {...}, warnings, notes}`; the `git` object also carries
`commit` (the current HEAD) for callers that deduplicate state.

`checkpoint`/`handoff` results carry `checkpoint.git.sync` with the same fields plus the top-level
`warnings`; `resume` returns `current_git.sync` and current warnings. The saved checkpoint under
`.agent-state/tasks/<task>.json` embeds `git.sync` in its `git` object. No command fetches, pushes,
commits, rebases, switches branches, opens a network connection, or starts an agent. Because no fetch
is performed, `ahead`/`behind` reflect local tracking refs and may be stale.

### `sync notify`

`sync notify` is the opt-in batch notifier for one or more repositories and their
worktrees. It is silent when clean, deduplicates identical state, and never
pushes, commits, or merges.

```bash
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync notify --project .
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync notify \
  --registry ~/.config/skill-atlas/projects.json --channel stderr
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync notify \
  --project ~/repos/one --project ~/repos/two --channel json
```

Flags: repeated `--project PATH`; `--registry PATH` (JSON list or an object with a
`projects` list); `--channel macos|stderr|json` (default `macos`); `--min-interval
MINUTES` (default 60); `--state PATH` (default
`~/.cache/skill-atlas/sync-notify.json`); `--fetch` (off by default; only updates
remote-tracking refs); `--fetch-timeout SECONDS` (default 10); `--include-dirty`
(off by default). Actionable conditions are no upstream, unpushed commits,
behind remote, and detached HEAD; dirty state is actionable only with
`--include-dirty`. At least one target is required.

`--channel json` returns `{status, channel, checked, notified, suppressed,
skipped, fetch_errors, state_file, fetch, notes}`. `status` is `notified` when at
least one worktree was newly actionable, otherwise `clean` (including when all
actionable states were suppressed). Each `notified`/`suppressed` entry has
`project`, `path`, `branch`, `has_upstream`, `ahead`, `behind`, `dirty`,
`detached`, `commit`, and `warnings`; `skipped` entries add `reason` and
`fetch_errors` entries add `error`. See [Sync Notifications](sync-notify.md) for
channels, deduplication, optional fetch, macOS caveats, and wiring examples.

See [Installation and Development Layout](development-layout.md#push-before-you-hand-off-and-during-long-work)
for recommended cadence, optional shell/scheduler/hook wiring, and the rule to never auto-push.

# Cross-Agent Context and Handoff

Use this workflow when configuring cooperation across agent tools, diagnosing missing shared context, or organizing project memory. Rule-entry setup is an agent-led workflow. Optional checkpoint, handoff, and resume CLI commands are documented below; they do not provide startup hooks or automatic model switching. A separate opt-in local transport (`message` commands, documented under [Agent Handoff Messages](agent-messaging.md)) queues compact handoff notes as files under `.agent-state/messages/<task>/`; it does not notify, wake, or start the recipient, and a person must approve any message marked `--requires-approval` before it can be recorded as completed.

## Discover before configuring

Identify the user's actual task, project root, relevant checkouts, participating tools, and their configured instruction sources. Inspect existing rules and state before proposing additions. A tool name, installed skill, symlink, or similarly named repository is not evidence of a working context handoff.

For local file evidence before configuring anything, run the read-only `agents scan` command (`python3 scripts/skill_atlas.py agents scan --project .`). It checks a reviewed catalog of agent tools, their rule and skill roots, shared physical skill roots, and local Skill Atlas copy versions, then reports file-evidence levels (`not-detected`, `detected`, `configured`). The scan never executes a tool, opens a network connection, reads credentials or session data, or writes anything; `configured` is not proof of runtime loading, and candidate paths stay unverified hints. Treat the result as discovery evidence and confirm the tool's own current documentation before changing configuration. See [Local Agent Environment Scan](agent-environments.md).

Before choosing a canonical checkout or reconciling project state, run the read-only `projects audit` command (`python3 scripts/skill_atlas.py projects audit --project . --project /path/to/other-copy`). It finds candidate project roots, groups likely-duplicate copies (normalized git remote = confirmed; case-folded directory name = probable), hashes agent-facing project documents without printing contents, and flags divergent documents and nested project roots. Its recommendations are plans only and require user confirmation; hashes prove difference, not which copy is authoritative. See [Project Root and Duplicate Documentation Audit](project-root-audit.md).

Separate these responsibilities:

| Layer | Purpose | Discovery examples |
|---|---|---|
| Shared general rules | Stable principles, preservation, model/tool selection, collaboration boundaries | A user-controlled rules file referenced or loaded by each tool |
| Tool entry | Load shared rules within that tool's own instruction hierarchy | Global instruction file or supported configuration |
| Project rules | Project constraints, workflows, validation, ownership conventions | Existing `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` |
| Project index | Map confirmed project roots to rules and state | Optional existing registry or a small user-approved Markdown index |
| Project state | Current objective, decisions, progress, evidence, blockers, next action | Existing `PROJECT_STATE.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, or equivalent |

An index is useful for multiple projects; do not introduce it for a single project without a concrete need. Reuse an established state file rather than forcing a new filename. Global context must not substitute an unrelated objective for the user's current project request.

Inspect each participating tool's current documentation, installed implementation, and configuration. Common entry candidates include Codex's global `AGENTS.md`, Claude Code's applicable `CLAUDE.md`, OpenCode's configured global `AGENTS.md`, and DeepSeek Harness's home `AGENTS.md`. These are discovery hints, not universal paths or proof of automatic loading. For Hermes and other tools, discover the supported entry rather than guessing.

Confirm environment overrides, instruction precedence, filesystem permissions, project-root discovery, and whether external file references are actually loaded. If references are not expanded, use a supported instructions setting or explicitly instruct the agent to read the target. Avoid copying complete rules into every tool entry when one maintained source is sufficient.

## WorkBuddy adapter discovery

The macOS WorkBuddy build inspected on 2026-10-30 exposes a user/project rules loader and a separate project-guidance loader. Treat these findings as version-specific discovery evidence, not proof of runtime loading on another installation.

- **User rules:** inspect the effective user configuration root and its `rules/` directory. In the inspected installation, the candidate was `~/.workbuddy/rules/`; Markdown `.md` and `.mdc` files are supported. Verify the root from the installed loader, configuration, or diagnostics before writing.
- **Rule metadata:** the inspected parser recognizes `alwaysApply: true` for always-applied rules and `enabled: false` to disable a rule. Use a small, independently named adapter rather than overwriting a user's existing rule.
- **Project guidance:** the inspected loader checks the task working directory in this order: `CODEBUDDY.md`, `.codebuddy/CODEBUDDY.md`, then `AGENTS.md`, taking the first readable file. Do not assume that all three are merged or that it searches parent directories. Inspect existing higher-priority guidance before relying on `AGENTS.md`.
- **Loading conditions:** guidance/rules injection depends on the request path and mode; quick/ask-like paths or previously injected context can skip relevant loaders. Verify a suitable fresh task rather than assuming every request reloads external edits.
- **Account and memory scope:** the application also has account-scoped user memory. It is a separate mechanism; do not overwrite memory files, databases, credentials, or account state to install a rules adapter. Check account/environment overrides when observed behavior differs from the configured path.

A minimal rule can use this shape, replacing placeholders with verified paths before installation:

```markdown
---
alwaysApply: true
---
# Shared collaboration entry

Before substantive work, use the file-reading tool to read <shared-rules-file>,
<project-index-if-used>, and the actual project's existing rules and state.
Preserve other agents' updates and record file scope before overlapping edits.
Report inaccessible paths and distinguish configured files from verified loading.
```

After configuration, use the verification levels below. Ask the receiving WorkBuddy task to identify the files it actually read and summarize the project's objective, current ownership, and next action. Do not dispatch that request without user authorization. If the application has not produced loading evidence, report **configured; loading unverified**.

For current product behavior, consult the installed implementation and [WorkBuddy project documentation](https://www.codebuddy.cn/docs/workbuddy/From-Beginner-to-Expert-Guide/Function-Description/Project); do not apply CodeBuddy CLI/IDE instructions to WorkBuddy solely because the products share a name or file convention.

For new rule/state files, adapt the [public collaboration templates](../templates/README.md). They provide three roles without containing live user records; reuse existing project files instead when available.

## Plan and apply a narrow integration

For a setup request, report the discovered entry paths, proposed shared source, project-state paths, exact additions, backup location, and rollback method. Respect explicit authorization already provided in the session; ask only for unresolved choices or required permissions. An audit or recommendation alone does not authorize writes.

Back up existing files before editing, re-read them before writing, and preserve concurrent updates. Add a small adapter to each supported tool entry and project routing only where needed. Preserve unrelated provider, model, plugin, credential, permission, and startup configuration. Do not replace existing symlinks or consolidate physical skill copies as an incidental part of context setup.

Keep paths configurable or discover them from the environment. Do not publish a user's absolute paths, private project details, credentials, or session transcripts in a reusable skill. Machine-local adapters may contain verified local paths.

## Maintain state while working

During authorized task execution, agents should read the actual project's rules and state, then maintain meaningful progress there. Keep state concise:

- objective and observable completion criteria;
- confirmed decisions, their rationale, and material assumptions;
- completed work and relevant evidence;
- unverified items, blockers, and next action;
- participating agents and file scope when work overlaps.

Use first-principles reasoning to choose execution: start from the outcome, facts, assumptions, and actual constraints, then select the simplest feasible approach. Assess models, tools, skills, and agent participation by task fit, available capabilities, quality, time, and cost. Multiple agents are optional; add them when independent work or review justifies coordination overhead. Verify current model claims rather than embedding a permanent model ranking.

Before overlapping edits, confirm current ownership and scope. Re-read shared state before updating it. Old assignments are historical evidence, not reliable live locks. Resolve overlapping changes before writing; do not switch another agent's branch or overwrite its work. A state-file update is a handoff record, not authorization to send a message or start work in another thread.

For historical context already mixing multiple projects, keep the source intact. Register confirmed project paths and place new detailed progress in the corresponding project state. Extract historical summaries incrementally with source pointers and uncertainty notes when requested; do not bulk move, delete, or rewrite history based on guessed ownership. Ask only when project identity cannot be safely determined.

## Verify the handoff

Distinguish evidence levels in the report:

1. **Configured:** entry files exist, referenced paths resolve, original content is preserved, and changes match the plan.
2. **Loaded:** a fresh request or supported diagnostic shows the target tool loaded the entry and read the relevant shared/project files.
3. **Handoff verified:** a receiving agent correctly identifies the project objective, decisions, current ownership, and next action from those files. An authorized disposable marker can test write-back when needed; never modify product state merely to prove connectivity.

Stop at the strongest supported claim. Do not infer runtime loading from file existence or claim live chat synchronization, model switching, task dispatch, or accepted assignments without tool evidence. Do not interrupt an active user session or send a cross-thread test prompt without authorization. When runtime verification is unavailable, finish the safe configuration and clearly record what remains unverified.

Keep setup reversible: retain backups outside managed skill trees, record every changed path, and restore only the intended change after checking for newer edits. Report platform-specific limitations rather than presenting one tool's behavior as universal.


## Integrated task checkpoints

This repository includes optional concrete local commands for
`checkpoint`, `handoff`, and `resume`. These commands persist a small
task-scoped JSON record in `.agent-state/tasks/<task>.json` and immutable
history records under `.agent-state/history/<task>/`.
They are complementary to an existing `PROJECT_STATE.md` or `CONTEXT.md`,
not an instruction to overwrite those files.

The command records Git state without storing a raw diff or session
transcript. If the new working tree or commit differs from the saved
snapshot, resume returns `review-required`; the receiving agent must
inspect the difference rather than assuming the previous work is valid.
The CLI does not start other agents, execute tests, write Git commits,
or transfer local files between machines. Actual automatic triggers
remain platform-specific.

The optional `message` commands add a local file-based transport on top of the
same `.agent-state/` tree, scoped per task. `message send` queues a compact
envelope; the addressed recipient reads it with `message inbox` or
`message show` and records `taken`, `completed`, or `refused` with
`message ack`. Messages sent with `--requires-approval` cannot be marked
`completed` until a person runs `message approve --by`. Envelopes are
immutable, receipts are append-only, the default TTL is 24 hours, and a
message chain stops at 10 passes. Messages never notify or start an agent,
never open a network connection, and stay out of Git (`.agent-state/messages/`) with no secrets in

# Installation and Development Layout

This page explains where each local copy of Skill Atlas belongs and which copy may be
edited. It is written for two audiences: people who install the skill and people (or
agents) who change it.

The short version: **the Git repository is the only source of truth.** A local
installation is a derived copy, and a local edit belongs in a checkout of the repository,
not in the copy an agent loads.

## Roles

| Role | Purpose | May be edited? | How it changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upstream repository | Source of truth; all changes land here through pull requests | Yes, on a branch | Commit, push, review, merge |
| Development checkout | Working copy used to create a branch; preferably one `git worktree` per task | Yes, on its task branch | Commit and push to the same upstream remote |
| Installation copy | Directory an agent tool loads the skill from | **No** | Update by fetching a reviewed commit or release tag |
| Archive | Frozen snapshot kept for history or recovery | **No** | Never; add a new archive instead of rewriting one |

A machine can have several directories, but only one of them is the repository, and only
one of them is the installation. Everything else is a development copy or an archive.
The same rules apply regardless of which agent tool starts the work: Codex, Claude Code,
DeepSeek Harness, OpenCode, WorkBuddy, Kimi Code, Cursor, TRAE, Qoder or another client.

## Example layout

Paths are examples, not requirements. Use whatever locations your tools allow.

```text
~/repos/skill-atlas/                     # upstream checkout, usually on main
~/.local/share/agent-skills/skill-atlas/ # installation copy loaded by agent tools
~/worktrees/skill-atlas-issue-42/        # development worktree for one task
~/archives/skill-atlas-2026-01-01/       # frozen snapshot, read-only
```

Agent skill entries normally point at one of these locations. For example a shared
`~/.agents/skills/skill-atlas` entry may be a symlink to the upstream checkout, while
individual tool entries may point at the installation copy. A symlink does not create a
new copy and does not change these roles; only its target matters.

## For people installing the skill

1. Install from a reviewed commit, a release tag, or your fork — not from an unpublished
   working tree.
2. Do not edit files in the installation copy. Local edits there are invisible to the
   upstream project, are lost on the next update, and make the installed version
   disagree with what other agents load.
3. Update by fetching and fast-forwarding the installation copy, or by re-running the
   installer against a reviewed source:

   ```bash
   git -C /path/to/installation fetch origin
   git -C /path/to/installation merge --ff-only origin/main
   ```

   If the installer manages the directory, prefer `install` and `manage self update`
   with their review and confirmation steps.
4. Report problems upstream (an issue or a pull request) rather than patching the
   installation copy.

## For contributors and agents

1. Keep the upstream checkout clean and on `main`; do not develop there.
2. Create one branch and one worktree per task. A worktree shares the repository's object
   store and remote configuration, so it is cheaper than a second clone and its history
   cannot drift:

   ```bash
   git -C /path/to/repo fetch origin
   git -C /path/to/repo worktree add /path/to/worktrees/skill-atlas-issue-42 \
     -b feat/issue-42-checkpoint origin/main
   ```

3. Work, test and commit inside the worktree. Push the branch to the same upstream remote
   and open a pull request:

   ```bash
   git -C /path/to/worktrees/skill-atlas-issue-42 push -u origin feat/issue-42-checkpoint
   ```

4. When the pull request is merged, remove the worktree and optionally the branch:

   ```bash
   git -C /path/to/repo worktree remove /path/to/worktrees/skill-atlas-issue-42
   git -C /path/to/repo branch -d feat/issue-42-checkpoint
   ```

5. Do not copy files between clones by hand, and do not continue work in a clone that is
   not connected to the same upstream remote. If two copies disagree, compare commits and
   document differences in the pull request; do not reconcile them by overwriting one
   copy with the other.

Agents that can only write inside a sandboxed workspace can place the worktree in that
workspace while the repository itself stays elsewhere. Creating the worktree writes only
the repository's `.git/worktrees/` metadata; the branch and commits are still pushed to
the upstream remote.

## Keeping an installation honest

A local installation can lag behind `main` while still reporting an old version, or a
development copy can be mistaken for the installation. The read-only
[agent environment scan](agent-environments.md) reports local Skill Atlas copies, their
versions and symlink aliases, and sets `version_mismatch` when copies disagree:

```bash
python3 /path/to/skill-atlas/scripts/skill_atlas.py agents scan --format json
```

Treat `version_mismatch: true` as a prompt to compare commits, not as permission to
overwrite a directory. The scan only reports file evidence; it does not prove which copy
an agent actually loaded.

## Archiving an old copy

When a copy is replaced, freeze it rather than deleting it immediately if it may contain
unique work:

1. Record its Git state: `git bundle create <name>.bundle --all`, plus
   `git status --porcelain` and a patch of uncommitted changes.
2. Archive the working tree, including untracked files.
3. Write a short provenance note: original path, date, version, commit, what was
   uncommitted, and how to restore it.
4. Record checksums and keep the archive out of every agent's skill roots.
5. Delete the original only after the archive has been verified and you have decided it
   is no longer needed.

An archive is evidence, not a development location and not an installation.


## Protect the integration branch

A development convention only works if the shared branch cannot be changed around it.
On GitHub, protect the branch that agents push to (usually `main`):

- **Require a pull request before merging.** Direct pushes bypass review, status checks and the history that later agents read.
- **Require the project's CI status check** (for this repository, the `python` job). A green check is evidence, not decoration.
- **Block force pushes and branch deletion.**
- **Include administrators.** Without this, an admin token (including an automation token) can bypass the rules. The protection then protects people from their own automation, not just from each other.
- Require conversation resolution when review comments are used.

Administrators can still disable protection in repository settings; that is an explicit, auditable action rather than a routine bypass. A solo maintainer pays a small cost: hotfixes also go through a pull request. That cost is usually smaller than recovering from an unreviewed or unverified push.

Hosts other than GitHub expose similar controls (protected branches, required checks, merge queues). The principle is the same: the integration branch accepts changes only through a reviewed, verified path.

## Push before you hand off (and during long work)

A local commit is not a handoff. Work that exists only in one checkout — an unpushed branch, a commit
with no upstream, or uncommitted changes — is invisible to another machine, another agent, or a
resumed session that reads the remote. Push reviewed work before handing it off.

Skill Atlas checkpoints and handoffs now record a read-only `git.sync` block in the saved state, and
their command results add a top-level `warnings` array so this risk is visible in the handoff
evidence:

- **no upstream** — the current branch has no upstream; commits are local-only;
- **ahead** — local commits are not on the remote;
- **behind** — the remote-tracking branch is ahead; fetch and then rebase or merge deliberately;
- **dirty** — uncommitted changes exist (the count excludes `.agent-state/`);
- **detached HEAD** — commits are not on a branch and are easy to lose.

`resume` reports the same current warnings when it inspects a saved checkpoint. To check on demand,
run the read-only sync command:

```bash
python3 /path/to/skill-atlas/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync status --project .
```

```text
# Git sync status
- branch: `feat/issue-42`
- upstream: `origin/feat/issue-42`
- ahead: 1; behind: 0; dirty: 0
- warning: 1 local commit(s) are not on the remote; push when the work is reviewed
- note: Read-only local Git status; no fetch, push or repository mutation executed
```

The command never fetches, pushes, commits, rebases, or changes a branch, and it opens no network
connection. `ahead` and `behind` are computed from local tracking refs, which may be stale until you
fetch yourself. Treat the warnings as prompts for a human decision, not as a blocked state.

Recommended checkpoints: when you save a checkpoint or handoff, at the end of a work block, before
switching agents, after a merge, and before leaving work another session may resume. This is **not a
background daemon and has no timer**: a reminder appears only when `checkpoint`, `handoff`, `resume`,
or `sync status` runs.

If you want a proactive reminder, wire the same read-only command into your own shell, scheduler, or
client hook. A portable shell function is enough:

```bash
# Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc; pass a project path or use the current directory.
sync_reminder() {
  python3 /path/to/skill-atlas/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync status --project "${1:-.}"
}
```

`cron`, `launchd`, and agent-client hooks can call the same command, but each platform's scheduler
and hook configuration differs; validate that yours runs and shows output. Do not auto-push from any
of these reminders.

A person decides what to do next: push only reviewed commits, never push credentials, private keys,
or large binaries, and when `behind` is reported fetch first and then rebase or merge deliberately.
Create a branch before continuing from a detached HEAD, and commit or explicitly discard local
changes before handoff.

### Lightweight notifications (`sync notify`)

`sync notify` runs the same checks across one or more repositories and every
worktree they contain, and notifies only when a worktree is actionable (no
upstream, unpushed commits, behind, detached HEAD; dirty only with
`--include-dirty`). It is still opt-in and one-shot — no daemon and no timer:

```bash
python3 /path/to/skill-atlas/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync notify --project .
python3 /path/to/skill-atlas/scripts/skill_atlas.py sync notify \
  --registry ~/.config/skill-atlas/projects.json --channel stderr
```

The default channel is a macOS notification (via `osascript`; macOS may show
"Script Editor" as the app and there are no custom buttons); `stderr` and `json`
are available for hooks and scripts. It is silent when clean and deduplicates
identical state per worktree through a local state file and `--min-interval`
(default 60 minutes). `--fetch` is off by default and only updates
remote-tracking refs; it never pushes, merges, or commits.

To make the reminder proactive, wire `sync notify` into your own shell alias,
Claude Code/Codex hook, or launchd/cron job. Keep hooks compact: notifications
themselves do not consume model tokens, but a per-turn hook that feeds output
back to the model can add context tokens. Never add an auto-push step. Concrete
hook/launchd examples and caveats are in [Sync Notifications](sync-notify.md).

## Limitations

- Example paths in this page are illustrative; platform conventions and agent tools
  differ.
- A worktree shares repository metadata but not uncommitted changes, stashes or local
  configuration such as hooks; review them separately.
- This page describes a collaboration convention. Skill Atlas does not move, adopt or
  repair copies automatically.

# Disk Usage Audit

`disk scan` audits the space that agent work produces locally: agent homes,
session transcripts, caches, plugins, attachments, project media, build
artifacts and Git objects. It was added in `0.9.0-beta`; since `0.9.1-beta` it
reports both apparent and allocated sizes, and `0.10.0-beta` adds an explicit,
opt-in Trash cleanup path.

Every result reports two sizes. **Allocated size** (`st_blocks × 512`) is the
real disk usage; **apparent size** (`st_size`) is the logical file length and
can be much larger for sparse files. When the two differ, sizes are printed as
`<allocated> allocated (<apparent> apparent)`. The largest-files threshold,
reclaimable ordering and risk totals all use allocated bytes.

The audit reads file metadata only. It never reads file contents, credentials,
session text or account data and never follows symlinks while walking a tree.
By default it never moves or deletes anything and every suggestion is a plan for
the user. Only the explicit `--apply --to-trash --confirm` combination moves
selected low/medium risk candidates into a trash directory; permanent deletion
and `rm -rf` are never used. Its job is to show where space goes and how risky
each candidate is before anyone cleans anything up.

## What the audit does and does not prove

The audit reports:

- which known agent roots exist under `--home`, plus any repeated `--root`
  directories and one optional `--project` directory;
- apparent and allocated sizes per root and per direct child entry, plus
  allocated totals per category;
- the largest files whose allocated size is at or above a size threshold
  (`--min-file-mb`, default 200 MB);
- a category and risk level for every reported entry;
- a **suggested review** list with one suggested action per category; and
- explicit limitations in every result.

With `--apply --to-trash --confirm`, it can also move selected low/medium risk
direct-child candidates into a trash directory and report the result.

The audit does **not** prove:

- how much disk space deleting an entry would actually free — allocated size is
  real disk consumption, but APFS clones, snapshots, hard links and filesystem
  behavior can still make reclaimable space differ;
- that moving a path to Trash frees space immediately — the space is released
  only after the Trash is emptied, and this tool never empties it;
- which size is meaningful for a given file — allocated size shows disk
  consumption, while apparent size shows logical length and can be far larger
  for sparse files;
- that a candidate is safe to remove or move to Trash — categories and risks
  are name-based heuristics, not an inspection of the data;
- that a large file is unused, stale, or duplicated;
- that the scan covers the whole machine — known roots are discovery hints, and
  linked roots or external volumes are not followed;
- that any suggested action has been or will be performed; in particular,
  `--apply` results are direct moves to Trash, not permanent deletion.

Missing or unreadable paths are skipped and reported; they do not abort the
audit.

## Quickstart

Run from any directory. Markdown is the default output.

```bash
# Audit the default known agent roots under the current user's home.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan

# Add explicit directories, for example large document or chat folders.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan \
  --root ~/Documents/ChatGPT --root ~/Documents/Codex

# Include a project checkout, lower the largest-file threshold, list more files.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan \
  --project . --min-file-mb 100 --top 30

# Machine-readable result for review notes or automation.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan --format json

# Opt-in: move selected low/medium-risk candidates to Trash. Review first.
python3 <skill-root>/scripts/skill_atlas.py disk scan --apply --to-trash --confirm
```

The command is safe to run repeatedly without `--apply --to-trash --confirm`:
it creates and changes no state.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--home PATH` | Home directory whose known agent roots are audited. Defaults to the current user's home. |
| `--root PATH` | Additional directory to audit. May be repeated. |
| `--project PATH` | Optional project directory to include in the audit. |
| `--top N` | Number of largest files to report, ranked by allocated size (default 15; bounded to 0–100). |
| `--min-file-mb N` | Report files whose allocated size is at or above this size in MB (default 200). `0` includes every file size. |
| `--max-entries N` | Per-root safety limit on filesystem entries (default 400000, minimum 1000). When hit, that root is marked truncated and its sizes are incomplete. |
| `--apply` | Opt-in move step. Requires `--to-trash` and `--confirm`; without all three flags nothing is moved. |
| `--to-trash` | Move selected low/medium risk candidates into the trash directory. Permanent deletion is not supported. |
| `--confirm` | Explicit confirmation for `--apply`. |
| `--risk low\|medium` | Cleanup risk to move. May be repeated. Default: `low`. High risk is not selectable. |
| `--trash-dir PATH` | Destination trash directory (default `~/.Trash`). Must already exist; mainly for tests and external volumes. |
| `--format markdown\|json` | Markdown report (default) or the full result object. |

`--root` and `--project` are added to the default scope. If one requested root
is inside another, only the outermost is scanned so space is not counted twice;
the skipped nested roots are listed in `nested_roots_skipped`. Requested roots
that do not exist are omitted rather than reported as empty.

| `claude-code` | Claude Code home | `.claude` | documented |
